articles.title: Off-Highway Brake & Friction Excellence is All-Italian

paras.en: Off-Highway Brake & Friction Excellence is All-Italian

SK Wellman, a company specializing in the production of brake and frictions components for off-highway, has a lively DNA. A historical reality in Orzinuovi (Bs), where the plant is still located, over the years it has undergone transformations and changes that have contributed to making it what it is today: an evolved company, able to grow in loyalty to the local Italian territory and to innovate its sector with creativity and flexibility worldwide. Today, as part of the CentroMotion Group and its Carlisle Brake & Friction division, SK Wellman is a leader in its segment, recognized and chosen by major brands in earthmoving, agricultural and construction machinery. Engineer Alessandro Gamba, Global Director of Friction Engineering, tells us about the ongoing growth.

paras.en: "S.K. Wellman S.R.L. has 340 employees and a turnover of 127 million by 2023," Gamba begins. In the last five years, a strong push has come from the market but above all from the characteristics of SK, such as creativity, innovation, flexibility, which, in the final analysis, are the result of the greatest wealth of this company: people". They are the ones who make the Brescia-based company an authentic and tenacious company, to the point of being able to export not only their products successfully, but also their skills and design skills to the other plants of the Carlisle Brake & Friction division. The year 2023, which has just ended, confirms a positive performance in turnover for sales revenues alone, recording a slight decrease of -5% compared to the previous exceptional 2022 financial year; A year, the latter, probably unrepeatable for many realities of the Brescia and non-Brescia economy. In fact, 2023 was undoubtedly the year of change that helped people develop a greater ability to manage uncertainty, accepting and dealing with unexpected situations with more resilience.

paras.en: "At the base of success there is a matrix organization developed thanks to group governance - explains the engineer -: a verticality driven on all functions and skills, able to define and guide processes on a global scale and generate best practices. And that's not all," adds Gamba, "we are one of the companies with the lowest level of turnover, and this allows us to transfer the experience of those who have been with us for a long time to young people, on whom we particularly focus. Added to this is a company population of 15 different nationalities, whose strong collaboration creates a truly serene working climate," says the HR Manager. It is no coincidence that the direction of growth is particularly social responsibility.

Two more rare gems for the metalworking industry? A level of accidents at work that borders on zero, and the centrality of talent development. Towards excellence and beyond.

articles.title: GM, Ford active safety engineers to speak during SCRS OEM Summit at SEMA Show
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: At the SEMA Show next month, active safety engineers from General Motors and Ford will provide a look behind the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety before, during, and after a collision.

They’ll speak during the second session of the Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ (SCRS) 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, titled “Engineering the Safety Benefit: From Requirements to Real-World Performance,” Thursday, Nov. 5, from 2–3 p.m.

It will follow an earlier session featuring National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Deputy Administrator Lee White from 12:30–1:30 p.m. White will examine vehicle safety priorities and the agency’s role in advancing safety on U.S. roadways.
To register for all three OEM Summit sessions, visit here.
An SCRS RDE Full Series Pass provides access to Tuesday and Wednesday RDE sessions, the IDEAS Collide Showcase, Thursday’s OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, and the SCRS Afterparty.

“This second session will move from those broader safety objectives into the vehicle itself, examining how automakers translate requirements and safety goals into technologies designed to produce measurable real-world benefits,” an SCRS press release states. “The afternoon will then progress to the collision repair environment, exploring how those engineered capabilities are preserved and restored after a vehicle has been damaged.”

The second session will bring together engineers who are responsible for developing, evaluating, and measuring advanced vehicle safety systems. Attendees will learn about the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety.

Panelists include Michael Carpenter, General Motors Active Safety and Global Vehicle Performance owner; Jameson Collins, General Motors Active Safety and staff product manager; and Jeremy Nelson, Ford Motor Co. ADAS application systems engineer.

Carpenter works within GM Global Product Safety, Systems, and Certification on ADAS technology and performance strategies, new technology development, implementation of regulatory and consumer metric requirements, ADAS field effectiveness and safety benefits, and industry collaboration on standards and test-method development.

Collins leads product strategy, roadmap development, and delivery for GM’s Active Safety features, translating customer needs, competitive insights, and regulatory requirements into technologies intended to improve safety and the driving experience.

Nelson focuses on the development, release, integration, and servicing of advanced driver assistance system domain controllers. He supports vehicle production and development milestones while troubleshooting ADAS components and working across engineering, quality, and product development teams to ensure systems perform safely and as intended.

The discussion will be moderated by Jake Rodenroth, automotive industry executive, and will move beyond what ADAS features do to examine why they exist, how their intended performance is established, and how their effectiveness is evaluated. This will include what it means when a safety system is absent, disabled, damaged, or operating outside its intended parameters.

The release states: “That progression leads directly to a fundamental question for collision repair professionals: If a vehicle entered a collision with a measurable safety capability, how can the repairer know that capability has been restored?”

The panel will also explore ADAS feature development, real-world effectiveness, crash avoidance and mitigation, implications of inoperable systems, verification of safety performance, and the potential for system degradation.
The 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit is part of SCRS’ Repairer Driven Education (RDE) program at the SEMA Show.

“The Summit brings collision repair professionals together with automakers, engineers, regulators, and other subject-matter experts to examine emerging technologies and their implications for safe and complete vehicle repair,” the release states.

During the first session, White will present on the agency’s current vehicle and roadway safety priorities, emerging transportation technologies, data-driven research, and the federal government’s work with the industry to reduce fatalities and serious injuries, an SCRS release states.

Following White’s presentation, he will sit down with Aaron Schulenburg, SCRS executive director, for a one-on-one conversation exploring the intersection between federal safety objectives, automotive innovation, and the collision repair industry’s role in preserving vehicle safety throughout its service life.
NHTSA sits at the center of many discussions that impact the collision repair industry.

During a July Collision Industry Conference meeting, Schulenburg discussed NHTSA’s investigation into counterfeit airbags with Teena Bohi, an Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council (A2C2) Board member.

In April, NHTSA announced a ban on one type of counterfeit airbag part. Before the ban, it also issued an “urgent” industry alert specifically asking the auto repair industry to look for dangerous airbag inflators.
Repair procedures are impacted by NHTSA-mandated vehicle safety technology. This includes mandated backup cameras in all new vehicles under 10,000 pounds as of May 2018.
NHTSA also has a final rule that mandates automatic emergency braking (AEB) in pedestrian vehicles by September 2029.
However, NHTSA also announced it paused the rule to give the Trump administration time to review it following pushback and a lawsuit filed by the Alliance of Automotive Innovation (Auto Innovators).
Additional information about SCRS and RDE can be found at www.scrs.come/rde
For more information about SCRS or to join as a member, visit www.scrs.com, call 877-841-0660, or email [email protected]

articles.title: Class action lawsuit filed against CCC alleging consumer personal information misuse
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: A class action lawsuit filed Oct. 8 in California against CCC Intelligent Solutions and CCC Intelligent Solutions Holdings alleges that CCC stores personally identifiable information (PII) from collision repair estimates created in CCC ONE to inform its artificial intelligence products and analytics.

The PII in question includes customer names, home addresses, phone numbers, insurance claim numbers, vehicle identification numbers, license plate numbers, and vehicle mileage. CCC also stores photos of damaged vehicles, according to the suit.
Plaintiffs LaTrenda Zekenya Burries, Gloribel Lissbeth Garcia, and Katleen Saturné were all involved in vehicle collisions and sought repairs at California collision repair facilities.
The suit alleges intrusion upon seclusion, invasion of privacy under the California Constitution, unjust enrichment, and violation of California’s unfair competition law.

The Law Offices of Maro Burunsuzyan, on behalf of the plaintiffs, says the alleged harm is the loss of privacy and control over personal information, including the ability to decide whether it could be repurposed and commercially exploited, as well as being deprived of resulting economic value.

CCC allegedly combines stored PII with data across its network to build AI products and analytics that it licenses to other customers without notice, consent, or compensation to the consumers who own the information, according to the complaint.
When Repairer Driven News asked CCC for comment on the suit, CCC replied that it “doesn’t comment on pending litigation.”

“Its contract with insurers provides that ‘CCC may use data to train AI Services,'” the complaint states. “Its contract with repair facilities reserves to CCC the use of the facility’s data for CCC’s own ‘product improvement, and research and development,’ a use that ‘may continue after the expiration or termination of this agreement.’ CCC tells consumers none of this. No page of the estimate describes CCC’s retention, aggregation, or commercial use of the personal information, or gives the consumer any way to opt out of it, see it, or delete it.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The suit adds that a repair facility’s contract with CCC doesn’t equal consumers’ consent for CCC to collect and use their data.
“CCC’s own contract anticipates as much by requiring the repair facility to indemnify CCC ‘for failure to obtain the requisite authorizations,'” the suit states.

The agreements noted in the suit are CCC’s Repair Facility License Agreement, effective in 2018; form Independent Appraiser Master License Agreement, reflected in a product schedule executed in 2024; the Insurer MSA, CCC’s public Master Services Agreement for insurers, last updated Nov. 7, 2025; and CCC’s companion Data Processing Addendum (DPA), last updated Nov. 4, 2025.

According to the suit, the Repair Facility License Agreement “authorizes CCC to provide the repair ‘content’ to insurers whose direct repair programs the shop participates in, or with whom the shop configures CCC ONE UpdatePlus to share information, and separately authorizes CCC to provide the Content to CCC’s vendor, Flash of Genius, Inc. (d/b/a UpdatePromise) (“Flash”), granting the identified insurers, CCC, and that vendor ‘perpetual, royalty-free licenses to use the content.'”
The agreement also “forbids the repair facility itself to ‘compile estimate data for the purpose of creating a database,’ a use that CCC reserves to itself…”

The Appraiser License Agreement also forbids the appraiser to “‘compile estimate data for the purpose of creating a database'” and “‘aggregate or co-mingle data in the programs and/or services or provide reports or analysis based on data in the programs and/or services to anyone.'”

It notes as well that a section of the Insurer MSA, titled “License by Customer to CCC,” “contemplates the development or testing of artificial intelligence tools or models on Customer Data that has not been de-identified, subject only to the customer’s prior written approval, which the provision states CCC may accept by e-mail from a vice-president-level or higher employee of the customer.”
The plaintiffs contend that consumers aren’t parties or signatories to the aforementioned agreements despite CCC’s collection, movement, and licensing of their personal information.

“The Repair Facility License Agreement runs between CCC and a collision repair facility, the Appraiser License Agreement runs between CCC and an independent appraiser, and the Insurer MSA and DPA run between CCC and an insurer,” the suit states.

“The only authorization CCC obtains to take and use consumers’ personal information under these agreements is the business’s own promise: under the Repair Facility License Agreement, customer ‘represents and warrants that it has full right and authority to provide the authorization and licenses contained herein,’ and indemnifies CCC ‘for failure to obtain the requisite authorizations;’ and under the Appraiser License Agreement, customer ‘represents and warrants that it has the right to provide the data to CCC.'”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The suit also states that CCC has patented training AI models on identifiable consumer data and harvesting vehicle event data recorder information, including U.S. Patent No. 10,922,726; U.S. Patent No. 11,727,551; and U.S. Patent No. 9,500,545.

“Taken together, these patents describe CCC’s designs for systems that ingest, store, retrain on, and reuse identifiable consumer and vehicle data of the kinds that populate CCC ONE, including names, home addresses, VINs, license plates, policy and claim identifiers, and event-data-recorder data,” the suit states. “On information and belief, CCC has implemented these designs in the CCC ONE platform and in the artificial-intelligence products and analytics it licenses to insurers and other customers.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The proposed nationwide class includes more than 15 million U.S. vehicle owners or customers named on repair estimates that a U.S. collision repair facility prepared on CCC ONE in the four years before the complaint was filed. It also proposes a nationwide intrusion subclass and a California subclass.

Relief sought includes nominal and punitive damages, restitution and disgorgement of the value CCC obtained from consumers’ information, barring CCC from using consumer information for AI training or other purposes beyond the estimate without consent, and requiring CCC to delete consumer PII.

An injunction on behalf of the California subclass would require CCC to inform California consumers before or when their personal information is entered into CCC ONE at a collision repair facility of its identity, the categories of PII it collects, and the purposes of use for the PII. It would also require CCC to obtain consumer consent before using PII for any purpose beyond preparing or transmitting vehicle estimates or valuations.
CCC hadn’t filed a response to the suit in court as of Monday afternoon.

“Artificial intelligence is reshaping the economy, and the question of what these systems are built on has never mattered more,” said Maro Burunsuzyan, attorney for the plaintiffs and founder of the Law Offices of Maro Burunsuzyan, in a press release.

“The complaint alleges that, in CCC’s case, part of the answer is the personal information of ordinary people who simply needed a car repaired. Those drivers were never told, never asked, and never paid. This case is about restoring a basic principle: a company that wants to profit from your information should have to ask you first.”

articles.title: Volvo research shows automaker has decreased injury for men and women by 79%
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: A new report from Volvo finds that equal protection for men and women can be achieved through data-driven safety development grounded in real-world crash research, the release states.
The research found that overall injury for drivers has decreased by 79% for Volvo models from 2010 to 2019 compared to models from 1970 to 1979.
Volvo saw an 88% decrease for women, bringing the injury risk to the same level as men, the release states.

“The results also show substantial advances in occupant protection across all seating positions,” the release adds. “Restrained rear-seat occupants in Volvo cars benefit from protection levels comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, those of front-seat occupants.”

Volvo says the data underscores the effectiveness of decades of rear-seat safety innovation in Volvo cars. This happened with the lack of regulatory requirements and standardized testing, the release states.

“For too long, safety in the automotive industry has not worked equally well for everyone,” says Åsa Haglund, Volvo head of Cars Safety Centre, in the release. “At Volvo Cars, we’ve taken a different approach. By studying real-world crashes and designing with the needs of women, men and children of all body types in mind, we’ve worked for decades to provide a high level of protection regardless of who you are or where you sit in the car. Our latest research confirms that equal protection is not just an ambition, but something we have been able to achieve in Volvo cars for many years.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Volvo has collected data since 1970 from more than 50,000 real-world crashes involving more than 80,000 occupants, the release notes. It adds that the insights are translated into safety requirements, testing, vehicle development, verification, and production.
“The result is a continuous cycle of learning that helps drive innovations and improve protection for everyone,” according to the release.
The study also reviewed different crash types. It found that frontal impact injuries were reduced by 79% for all drivers. Side impacts saw a larger reduction in injuries at 89%.

The approach also laid the foundation for pioneering Volvo Cars Safety Standard, according to the release. Through the standard, Volvo sets its own benchmark for real-world safety, going beyond regulation or safety ratings, Volvo says.

“And because real-world crashes don’t involve standardized crash test dummies, Volvo Cars’ research involves considering a diverse range of occupant characteristics, including gender, height, body shape and weight,” the release states. “As a result, the company’s safety innovations are designed with the same diversity in mind.”

Volvo notes it has openly shared its safety research to help raise safety standards across the industry through the Equal Vehicles for All (E.V.A.) initiative launched in 2019. It adds that more than 50 years of safety research is freely accessible in a digital library. Carmakers, researchers and policyholders can use the data to build on Volvo’s insights.

The recent study focuses on a broad range of real-world crash scenarios, including frontal, side, and rear-end impacts; run-off-road collisions; rollovers; side-swipe collisions; large animal impacts; and multi-collision crashes.

It also focuses on belted occupants aged 13 or older and examines injuries with moderate potential to threaten life, such as fractures and concussions, while excluding minor injuries such as bruises and pain.
Earlier this year, Volvo introduced a new seatbelt that adapts to traffic variations and the person wearing it via real-time data.
The Volvo EX60 was the first vehicle equipped with the multi-adaptive seatbelt.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) released research in January that found women are at higher risk of injury than men in collisions. The research followed details released by the U.S. Department of Transportation on an advanced female crash test dummy.

articles.title: Hunter Updates HawkEye XL Commercial Alignment System
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Hunter Engineering announced four new enhancements to its HawkEye XL Commercial Alignment System.
The new enhancements include (with descriptions by the company):

1) Magnetic wheel adapters – These adapters provide increased wheel protection, with no metal spades to get between the rim and tire, the company says. The adapters are available as an option for new and existing HawkEyeXL aligners.

2) Drive-through sensor configuration – The new configuration will allow drive-through shops and OEM production to skip repositioning their equipment for each alignment. The sensors offer the same long-range vision and field of view, with up to 16-foot-wide tower spacing to accommodate commercial vehicles.

3) New WinAlign software – Hunter’s latest WinAlign 18.3 software offers new target placement guidance to help the technician, aligner placement guidance so the cameras can easily see all the wheel targets, and the flexibility to perform thrustline and frame-reference alignments as desired.

4) Latest-generation alignment cart – Technicians can store adapters and control the alignment system from the rear of the vehicles. The cart is completely untethered with a battery backup, allowing a full day’s work without carrying a cable around the shop, the company says.
The XL handles heavy-duty, medium-duty, light-duty and passenger vehicles.

articles.title: MotoRad CEO Matt Buchholz on Aligning Values
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: This episode of DriveTime features Matt Buchholz, CEO of MotoRad. In this interview, Buchholz described how the company’s D.R.I.V.E. core values — Dedication, Relationship, Innovation, Value Driven and Expertise — provide the cultural foundation for how its team operates internally and engages with customers and channel partners.

Buchholz emphasized that culture and strategy are closely connected. By aligning teams around common values and empowering employees to live them every day, he said MotoRad creates a foundation for continuous improvement — reflecting his philosophy that when an organization gets better, it gets bigger.

As MotoRad expands across thermal management, emissions and powertrain controls, Buchholz said investment decisions begin with market intelligence and listening directly to customers. The company looks for opportunities that fit its existing capabilities and strategy while addressing clear market needs. Buchholz said it also evaluates adjacent categories for “low friction” opportunities where it can create value quickly. In many cases, some of MotoRad’s strongest product ideas have originated with technicians, counter professionals and other customers who identify ways the company can improve a product or make a repair easier.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Looking ahead, Buchholz said MotoRad’s growth strategy centers on three areas: commercial execution, operational agility and technology. Commercially, the company plans to continue listening to the market, responding faster and creating greater value through areas such as coverage, service, business intelligence and quality. Operationally, MotoRad is focused on diversifying its global supply chain to maintain continuity of supply and become nimbler. Technology supports both priorities by improving efficiency, reducing waste and helping the company respond to rapidly increasing expectations for speed.

articles.title: Battery Thermal Management Market to Hit $10.97B by 2033
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The battery thermal management system (BTMS) market is projected to grow from $5.26 billion in 2026 to $10.97 billion by 2033 at a CAGR of 11.1%, according to MarketsandMarkets. Increasing battery energy density, fast-charging requirements, higher power output, and stringent battery safety requirements are driving value and technology intensity in BTMS.

OEMs are transitioning from conventional air cooling toward liquid-cooled and integrated thermal architectures to manage battery temperature with greater precision and efficiency. Technology is also shifting toward AI-based thermal simulation, cell-level temperature monitoring, direct cell cooling, and intelligent controls, particularly for high-voltage 800V EV platforms requiring faster charging and tighter thermal uniformity. 800V BTMS solutions are being developed with higher coolant flow, faster preconditioning, and integrated battery heating and cooling to manage higher charging loads, according to the MarketsandMarkets report.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MAHLE Expands Battery Cooling Plate Production in Spain

In June 2026, MAHLE started series production of battery cooling plates at its Montblanc plant in Spain to support growing demand for liquid-cooled battery systems. The company plans to increase production from around 1,000 units per week to 8,000 units per week by the end of 2026, with the facility capable of reaching up to 15,000 units per week.

The cooling plates use optimized coolant channels to distribute heat uniformly across the battery and maintain operating temperatures below 40°C. MAHLE is also expanding the production area by around 10,000 m², supporting higher-volume production of battery thermal management components.
Webasto Develops Heated Chiller for Integrated Thermal Management

In December 2025, Webasto developed its Heated Chiller to combine battery cooling, battery heating, and cabin heating within a single thermal management unit. The system integrates the chiller, battery heater, and interior heater, reducing component count and simplifying thermal system integration.

The architecture supports coordinated temperature control across the battery and cabin, enabling battery preconditioning for charging while also meeting cabin heating requirements. Webasto is positioning the Heated Chiller as a compact thermal management solution for electric vehicles, with the technology progressing toward production applications.
BEV Segment Expected to Lead Global BTMS Market

The BEV segment is expected to have the largest share in the global BTMS market. BEVs are expected to be the fastest-growing vehicle type, as they account for more than 50% globally, supported by higher battery energy density, tighter cell temperature-control requirements, and greater integration of battery and vehicle thermal systems.

Within passenger BEVs, NMC batteries require active thermal control as higher energy density and charging power increase heat generation and cell temperature variation. This supports liquid cooling, direct cell cooling, battery preconditioning, and active temperature control. OEMs and BTMS suppliers are focusing on integrated and actively controlled thermal architectures.

For instance, the Mercedes AMG GT 4-Door Coupe uses direct cooling of cylindrical NCMA battery cells, with intelligent thermal management controlling cell temperature during high-power operation, while Bosch provides intelligent battery temperature control and diagnostics for BEVs.

These developments are increasing the need for optimized coolant distribution, low-thermal-resistance cooling structures, and coordinated thermal control across the battery, heat pump, HVAC, electric motor, and power electronics. High energy density batteries and higher charging power are supporting demand for advanced active BTMS solutions, particularly for NMC-based passenger BEVs.

articles.title: WAI Global Expands Late-Model Aftermarket Coverage
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: WAI Global expanded late-model aftermarket coverage to address evolving vehicle and application needs. In the third quarter of 2026, WAI Global introduced 124 new part numbers. These additions provide 100% new coverage for more than 52.3 million vehicles in operation across the United States and Canada.

The third-quarter introductions broaden WAI Global’s aftermarket portfolio across several key product categories. These include alternators, starters, wiper motors, window regulators, voltage regulators, brake calipers, solenoids, sensors and motors. The additions address coverage gaps, improve parts availability and support changing aftermarket demand.

“Our NPI strategy remains focused on identifying meaningful coverage gaps and bringing late-model and first-to-market solutions to customers quickly,” said Ron Bernstein, president, North America, WAI Global. “Adding coverage for more than 52 million vehicles this quarter reflects the scale of that effort and helps our customers stay ahead of changing vehicle populations and replacement demand.”
Notable late-model releases introduced during the quarter include:
- 30884N Starter: Up to 2026 Subaru Impreza
- 41012N Alternator: Up to 2025 Toyota RAV4
- WPM5036 Wiper Motor: Up to 2026 Hyundai Santa Fe and Tucson
- MAF20365 MAF Sensor: Up to 2026 Toyota Corolla and Sienna
- 380448 Window Regulator: Up to 2026 Subaru Ascent
Product Development Focuses on Coverage Gaps

The 124 new part numbers span multiple product categories and reflect WAI Global’s ongoing product development strategy. The latest additions prioritize late-model applications while expanding WAI Global’s 100% new aftermarket offering.

articles.title: Automotive Parts Headquarters Raises $513K for WACOSA
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Automotive Parts Headquarters Inc. (APH), together with its supplier partners and the Bartlett family, raised $513,000 through its annual fundraiser benefiting WACOSA, a central Minnesota nonprofit serving adults with disabilities. The 2026 event brings the fundraiser’s 14-year total to $3.7 million.
Proceeds support WACOSA programs that provide meaningful employment, day services and opportunities for more than 650 adults with disabilities across central Minnesota.

The event began with a walleye shore lunch and guided tours of WACOSA before attendees gathered at APH’s newest facility (a bulk storage warehouse) in St. Cloud for a pie and ice cream social celebrating its grand opening and APH’s “Building Our Future Together” initiative.

Attendees also participated in a hands-on art experience led by WACOSA artist-in-residence Dan Mondloch. The individual pieces created during the event will be incorporated into a collaborative collage inspired by the northern lights above a Minnesota lake.

“The day captured so much of what makes this event special,” said Jason Vogel, president of APH Stores Inc. “Bringing our supplier partners, employees and friends together to experience WACOSA’s mission firsthand, celebrate a new chapter for APH and create something together was incredibly rewarding.”

The day concluded with a cocktail reception, lobster-themed dinner and awards ceremony hosted by John and Nancy Bartlett at their home. A highlight of the evening was the presentation of a $513,000 check to Nancy Betts, executive director of WACOSA.

“Fourteen years of support from APH, its supplier partners and the Bartlett family has created a remarkable legacy for the people we serve,” Betts said. “This generosity creates opportunities for people to discover their strengths, contribute to their communities and pursue greater independence. We are deeply grateful for the lasting difference this partnership makes.”
Corey Bartlett, CEO and owner of APH, said the event reflects the generosity and commitment of the automotive aftermarket community.

“Every year, this event reminds us of the extraordinary generosity within the automotive aftermarket,” Bartlett said. “What began as a fundraiser has grown into a lasting partnership between APH, our supplier community and WACOSA. Seeing everyone come together to support the people and mission at the heart of WACOSA is what makes this event so meaningful.”
To view highlights from this year’s event, including the celebration, collaborative art project and messages from industry leaders, visit https://vimeo.com/autopartshq/wacosa26.

articles.title: Value Added: Creating a Culture Beyond Cost
articles.author: Thomas Dayton

paras.en: In case you haven’t noticed, the parts business is a pretty crowded marketplace. In my own little hometown of less than 30,000 people, we have EIGHT parts stores! There are also eight OEM dealer franchises, so there is certainly no lack of options for purchasing auto parts and supplies in our area… and that doesn’t even include online options. With 16 places offering parts in the immediate area, if we want to make a sale we have to make our offerings more attractive than everyone else.

In order to stand out in a crowded market, your operation needs to add value to your products beyond whatever your competitors are offering. That “value” may take the form of different things to different consumers, but this sort of “it factor” is integral to making you stand out in a crowd. Since there are so many kinds of added value, identifying those things your customers value can be challenging.

The Value Stick may sound like some off-brand deodorant, but it’s a concept endorsed by Harvard Business School to visualize the four factors that help build a value-based business strategy. At the top of the stick is a customer’s “willingness to purchase” (WTP), and at the bottom lies your own “willingness to sell” (WTS). In between the two are your cost and the selling price of a product. These four markers are all, to some degree, moveable up or down The Value Stick. WTS primarily concerns the vendors who supply your parts and employees who provide labor for your store. It is the lowest price at which you can purchase your stock and pay someone to sell and distribute it to your customers. WTP, on the other hand, depends solely on a customer’s estimation of your product’s value, and represents the maximum amount of money they will hand over for your product at the point of sale.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Price can be a funny thing. For some, a higher price signals an increase in quality over a less-expensive product (brand name vs. generics, for example), or the cache of luxury (they’d pay $50 more for a Tommy Hilfiger shirt than a similar garment from Wal-Mart). For others, a higher price only means your business is making excessive profits… at their expense. (“I can buy the same thing on Amazon for $20 less than your price, why are you so high?”)

I believe that many of our customers (professional and amateur alike) still view the products we sell daily as interchangeable commodities. As parts professionals, we know better, but when we are faced with those customers for whom “any old thing will do,” we have to use other means to attract them to spend their money with us. Of the four variables along the Value Stick, WTP is the one we have the most influence over. Short of renegotiating supplier prices or reducing staffing costs, we don’t have much control over the cost of our inputs. We must maintain a reasonable margin in order to pay our overhead and keep ourselves in business, so deeply discounting prices is not a long-term solution. The only remaining way to move the needle is to increase the value of our product. Not the individual gasket, chassis part, or alternator, but rather through the experience of purchasing it from us.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All else being equal, people buy from the people and places they know and trust. It is easier to build these kinds of relationships with commercial customers simply because of the volume of their business. We have more opportunities to show them that we are an important partner in their success, and that we value that partnership. Prompt delivery, complete and accurate order fulfillment and ease of doing business are all value-added services that help justify a premium price tag. For the more occasional customer (professional or retail), we have a shorter window of opportunity to make a lasting impression. Superior customer service is still our greatest advantage with this sort of customer. Employing a knowledgeable and friendly staff, or even utilizing online lookup and ordering platforms can streamline the buying process for customers who value convenience.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Many retailers also build value into their product offering by providing additional services like code-reading, battery testing and installation, or loaner tool programs. Geared toward the non-professional segment of their customer base, these services also position the retailer as a trusted partner in maintaining personal vehicles. Adding value beyond the cost and quality of your parts increases retention and creates a scenario in which satisfied customers become advocates for your business. Give them something no one else can, and they have no reason to go anywhere else.

articles.title: Get Smart: Processes for Continuous Improvement
articles.author: Thomas Dayton

paras.en: Continuous improvement is a business strategy aimed at providing superior customer service through the implementation of a series of small changes in your operations and policies. These individual improvements may be centered around efficiency, productivity, employee happiness, or a multitude of other factors, but, ultimately, their purpose is to make your operation better at attracting, serving and retaining customers.

Continuous improvement is most closely associated with the Japanese word Kaizen. The post-World War II rebuilding of the Japanese industry led to several advances in manufacturing efficiency and quality control, many of which were the basis for “modern” manufacturing and business concepts like “lean” or “just-in-time” manufacturing, Six-Sigma quality control and improvement, and “The Toyota Way.” Each of these concepts has its own variation on identifying potential roadblocks to success, proposing solutions, implementing the means to those solutions, and analyzing the success or failure of any changes made.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Know your customer: by understanding the customer’s needs and wants, you can implement improvements that matter to them.
Let it flow: removing barriers to efficiency and reducing waste creates a smooth workflow.
Go to where the work happens: don’t manage from an office, see the problem firsthand.
Empower people: improvements and the resulting success require input from the “bottom up.”
Transparency: share plans, goals, and results with the entire team.

These principles can be applied to any problem in your operation, but continuous improvement is often used initially in smaller, incremental stages. These small changes are easier to implement, as they do not require a complete overhaul of company culture or the involvement of the entire staff. These can be “experimental” changes on a small scale, to test their effectiveness in specific situations or with a particular department. Breakthrough continuous improvements are larger in scale, and are most effective when a process or operation is in need of a complete overhaul. In either situation, proposed improvements should align with these five principles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In order to transform the vague idea of a potential improvement into a clear plan of action with defined results, continuous improvement plans often rely on setting “SMART” goals. SMART is an acronym for “Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Timely.” SMART goals are a litmus test for determining if what you want to achieve is realistic and worthwhile to spend the time, energy, and money pursuing. Have you set a specific goal that accurately reflects the improvement(s) which you are hoping to implement? Can you measure the progress in a clear and meaningful way, so you know where you are in the process and know when you have achieved the goal? Is the improvement achievable with your current staff and resources? Are the changes relevant to your operation’s mission, values, and culture? And finally, is the goal time-sensitive? A goal without a deadline is more of a dream.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Once your organization has committed to continuous improvement and SMART goals have been set, the next step is to create and standardize the processes you want to use in working toward those goals. Staff must be given the tools (and the training) to implement any intended changes, and also an opportunity to express constructive opinions concerning the “real-world” effectiveness of the improvements. Project leaders should monitor the progress of each improvement project throughout the process and measure the results using key performance indicators (KPIs) tied to the results you hope to achieve through the planned changes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If the process yields positive results, you are (as an organization) one step closer to achieving your goal of serving your customers more effectively. Share your successes with those who helped create them, with others in the organization who may benefit from the discovery, and, most importantly, with the customers whom you are doing this for in the first place!

articles.title: This 850-year-old 'firework' supernova is full of mysterious knots
articles.author: Jamie Carter

paras.en: Where it is: 7,500 light-years away, in the constellation Cassiopeia
A mysterious "guest star" recorded by medieval astronomers nearly 850 years ago has revealed new secrets after scientists obtained the clearest images yet of its explosive aftermath.

New observations of Pa 30, thought to be the leftovers of a historic supernova called SN 1181, show that its spectacular firework-like filaments are not smooth streams of material. Instead, they consist of chains of tiny gas knots.

SN 1181 is so called because astronomers in China and Japan recorded its brief appearance in the year 1181, when they saw it as a naked-eye object in the constellation Cassiopeia. Eight surviving texts date its appearance to between Aug. 4 and 6 of that year. The mysterious object remained visible for 185 days.

"It's rare to get this level of detail on a supernova we can date to a specific week in history," Timothy Cunningham, an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Warwick who led an international team of researchers to study the object, said in a statement.

SN 1181 is one of only five supernovas in the Milky Way galaxy known to have been witnessed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. (Those optical instruments first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608.) Now, advanced ground-based telescopes can produce wonderfully detailed images of those historic remnants. This latest image is from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii and reveals about 10 times more filamentary structures in Pa 30 than have been seen before. This extraordinary detail gives astronomers fresh clues about the unusual explosion and the environment surrounding the star.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "These images give us the clearest picture yet of Pa 30's structure, and it's not what we expected," said Cunningham, whose team published their findings in The Astrophysical Journal. "The filaments are made of chains of tiny knots rather than smooth streaks, providing new constraints on the nature of the space around the star before it exploded and the physical processes that have shaped the expanding ejecta."
The knot-like structures may have resulted from variations in temperature or density in material surrounding the star as debris from the explosion expanded.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
- A star 20 times the size of the sun died in a supernova — and telescopes around the world joined forces to watch it
- Scientists mapped the shape of a supernova for the first time ever – and it's not what we expected: Space photo of the week
- Scientists find evidence of 'supernova graveyard' at the bottom of the sea — and possibly on the surface of the moon

Pa 30 contains another unusual feature: a surviving star that sits almost exactly at the center of the remnant. That's highly unusual, because a supernova explosion typically sends stars away from their original positions. It suggests that the original explosion was highly symmetrical, the researchers said.

Furthermore, Pa 30 is thought to be a Type Iax supernova. Unlike standard Type Ia supernovas, which destroy their stars, a Type Iax event is a lower-energy, incomplete explosion of a white dwarf star that can leave behind a remnant known as a "zombie star." It's the only Type Iax supernova ever found.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

articles.title: Black Death had dramatic effect on species diversity as humans abandoned farmland, study finds
articles.author: Sarah Wild

paras.en: When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes.

The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317.

This was followed by the Black Death, an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century.

The Black Death era is the perfect opportunity to look at the effects of humans on biodiversity over a longer period, Jonathan Gordon, a paleoecologist at the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York and first author of the paper, told Live Science.

In the study, which was published March 4 in the journal Ecology Letters, the researchers compared more than 100 European pollen records that included about 4,600 samples. The records came from sites ranging from the lowlands of France and uplands of the southwest United Kingdom to the Swiss Alps.
The pollen records "give us information on the past diversity of the plant records," Gordon said.

For example, cereal grains — such as wheat, barley and rye — were a fundamental part of medieval agriculture. The representation of pollen from these types of crops in the pollen record points to historic land use.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers divided the pollen data into three categories based on the presence of cereal pollen: places where agricultural production went up, places where it went down, and places where there was no evidence of cereal cultivation.
"We found a decline in biodiversity overall, but the decline overall was driven by those landscapes that declined in agricultural production," Gordon said.

"In those landscapes where agricultural production went down, there was a reduction in biodiversity of around 40%. Then, after about 150 years, as populations started recovering and landscape disturbances started increasing again, biodiversity went up to slightly above the level it was before."

Many people think there was a "stable and pristine world in which the entry of people has only one result: net loss of species and homogenization," Erle Ellis, an agroecologist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "The paleoecologists have always known the story is far more complicated."

There is a growing body of evidence showing that people's long-term cultural shaping of their landscapes often creates more diverse habitats, known as "mosaics," that can sustain more species than simple homogenous landscapes can, he said.
Whereas modern agriculture focuses on single crops on plots of land, in previous centuries, "you had all these different types of agriculture operating within the same landscape," Gordon said.

"In that landscape, you had lots of natural features that remained from the Middle or Early Holocene (which began after the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago)," he added. "You had old bits of woodland, you had heaths, you had ponds, and bits of secondary forest. It was all interlaced with these agricultural mosaics, and that led to raised biodiversity because there were more habitats for different plant species to exploit."

The findings highlight the differences between medieval and modern land use practices — and their consequences for biodiversity. Research suggests that during the 20th century, global biodiversity declined by up to as much as 11% and human activities, such as land-use changes, pollution, and climate change, are the major culprits. In agriculture, the practice of monoculture — where a single crop species is grown over a large area — reduces biodiversity.

"What this work contributes to showing is that, until relatively recently, even in Europe, very different forms of land management and interaction were practiced than exist today," Patrick Roberts, director of Department of Coevolution of Land Use and Urbanisation at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, told Live Science in an email.
- Aspen trees provide a natural buffer against wildfires, even as fire season intensifies, study shows
- Extreme heat waves are making our cities buckle. Investing in urban nature is no longer optional.
- 66 billion trees have been planted in China's Great Green Wall — and they appear to be growing faster than natural forests

"Rather than the monoculture, plantations, or uniform changes to landscapes we see in the 20th and 21st centuries, emphasis was placed on maintaining 'mosaics,'" said Roberts, who was not involved in the new research.

In the study, "we can see how relationships between people and biodiversity have changed through time and how people can actively use landscapes while maintaining biodiversity and mixed ecosystem functions," he said.

There is still more to understand about how humans' disappearance from landscapes in the Black Death era affected the natural world, Gordon said. "There are a lot of other types of diversity — not just the number of types, but what the different types present actually do." There may be a hundred types of plants in a landscape, but if they do the same thing, "you have low functional diversity," he said.

Functional diversity "is super important for how ecosystems adapt to changes in climate and how resilient they are, which is something we need for future-proofing our agricultural system," Gordon said.

Gordon, J. D., Fagan, B., Finch, J., Gillson, L., Milner, N., & Thomas, C. D. (2026). Black death land abandonment drove European diversity losses. Ecology Letters, 29(3), e70325. https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.70325

Sarah Wild is a British-South African freelance science journalist. She has written about particle physics, cosmology and everything in between. She studied physics, electronics and English literature at Rhodes University, South Africa, and later read for an MSc Medicine in bioethics.

Since she started perpetrating journalism for a living, she's written books, won awards, and run national science desks. Her work has appeared in Nature, Science, Scientific American, and The Observer, among others. In 2017 she won a gold AAAS Kavli for her reporting on forensics in South Africa.

articles.title: 'A uniquely direct route that might cause damage': Scientists uncover link between air pollution and eye diseases like glaucoma
articles.author: Sanket Jain

paras.en: Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions.

Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide, is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness.

Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. The research, presented in September at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons in London, brought together evidence from dozens of studies collectively involving millions of people across East Asia and the U.K.

The studies were observational, meaning they can only draw a link between air pollution and the eye conditions, rather than prove that air pollution causes the diseases. But still, "this reframes glaucoma and cataract as conditions shaped by where you live and breathe, not just how long you've lived," said study co-author Dr. Ahmed Alnabihi, an ophthalmologist at King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center in Saudi Arabia, who presented the findings. These environmental exposures may compound age-related decline in the eye as they do in cardiovascular disease, he said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The researchers examined exposure to several pollutants, including different sizes of particulate matter (PM), such as fine PM2.5 and larger PM10. They also looked at nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide.

Most studies included in the review estimated people's long-term exposure based on the pollution levels around their homes and in their communities. They used a range of methods, including government monitoring systems, satellite data and computer models designed to estimate pollution levels. A few studies examined short-term exposure and its relation to more sudden eye issues, such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency that can quickly cause vision loss.

Using this wealth of data, the team compared pollution exposure with rates of glaucoma, cataracts and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), another common eye condition that impairs vision. PM2.5 — tiny particles that measure 2.5 micrometers or smaller — showed the clearest associations with glaucoma and cataract risk.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

People with the highest exposure to PM2.5 had 70% higher odds of glaucoma, compared to those with the least exposure. Plus, an increase in PM2.5 exposure equivalent to the difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles of exposure within each study was associated with 8% higher odds of glaucoma and a 4% higher hazard of cataracts.

The evidence was less consistent for air pollution and age-related macular degeneration, which damages the central part of the retina that's responsible for sharp, detailed vision. And unlike the clear connection seen with PM2.5, other pollutants showed less consistent links to eye disease. For instance, nitrogen dioxide was not significantly tied to AMD, ozone was not tied to cataracts, and neither pollutant was linked to glaucoma. Sulfur dioxide and PM10 showed no significant associations with any of the three conditions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The association between PM2.5 and glaucoma was relatively consistent across the reviewed studies, said Nidhi Singh, an environmental epidemiologist at the IUF-Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine in Germany, who was not involved in the study. The findings for PM2.5 and cataracts were moderately consistent, albeit more variable than the glaucoma data; still, she said that the analysis seems to support a link.

Singh did caution that the underlying evidence is observational. "Therefore, the results demonstrate an association, not by themselves a causal effect of PM2.5 on glaucoma or cataract," she told Live Science.

The exact biological mechanisms behind these links remain unclear, but Alnabihi noted that fine particulate matter is small enough to be absorbed into the body. This can trigger oxidative stress, in which harmful molecules overwhelm natural defenses and cause damage. It also drives chronic, low-grade inflammation, in which the immune system stays mildly activated for long periods, he explained.
In the eye's lens, these processes can "damage the crystallin proteins that keep it transparent, causing them to misfold and cloud, which is what a cataract is," Alnabihi said.

In the optic nerve, the same processes are thought to damage retinal ganglion cells, a special type of neuron that relays information from the retina to the brain. This can contribute to glaucoma independent of internal eye pressure, he said, which is another big risk factor.
"Unlike the lungs or gut, its [the eye's] surface is in direct, continuous contact with outdoor air, giving pollutants a uniquely direct route that might cause damage," he added.
- 'Wildfire smoke is the fastest-growing environmental threat in the US': How a warming world will poison the air we breathe
- China's huge push to reduce air pollution had an unexpected consequence in the Arctic
- Pollution may fuel depression, anxiety and other mental health problems, emerging research suggests

Other studies have found clues that support the link between PM2.5 and eye damage. Mice that were exposed to ambient PM2.5 for nine months developed elevated pressure inside their eyes, a glaucoma risk factor. The researchers observed both oxidative stress and nitrative stress — a similar phenomenon — in the tissues that drain fluid from the eye, which may help to explain the rise in pressure.

Studies of humans and human cells have uncovered similar patterns. In data from more than 480,000 people in the UK Biobank, a large repository of health information, those exposed to higher PM2.5 were more likely to develop glaucoma over time. In another study, scientists exposed lab-grown human retinal tissue made from stem cells to PM2.5. The particles disrupted retinal cell development, including that of retinal ganglion cells, while increasing cell death.
These studies offer pieces of a possible mechanism, but for now, how those pieces fit together in people remains unclear.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Sanket Jain is an independent journalist and documentary photographer based in Western India’s Maharashtra state. Sanket’s work has been featured in over 35 publications, including MIT Technology Review, Devex, Wired, Telegraph, Thomson Reuters Foundation, The Nation, British Medical Journal, Verge, USA Today, Progressive Magazine and others. He was the winner of the 2025 Eric and Wendy Schmidt Award for Excellence in Science Communications. He was awarded an honorable mention for the 2026 Evert Clark/Seth Payne Award, which recognized a Live Science article and three others that addressed the impacts of air pollution and extreme heat on physical and mental health.
