articles.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%

paras.en: NASAâs Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%

- NASAâs Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. Romanâs Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.

The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.

"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test

Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.

Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.

Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.

Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.

"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.

The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.

"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."

Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.

"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair

Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.

"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.

The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.

The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.

Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.

To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.

That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."

With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure and evolution of the universe.

articles.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut

paras.en: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
A promising new drug reversed severe fatty liver disease in animals by healing the gut, revealing a surprising new path toward treating liver damage.
- Michigan Medicine - University of Michigan

- Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.
An experimental drug developed at Michigan Medicine has reversed a serious form of fatty liver disease in animal studies by targeting an unexpected source of liver damage: the gut.

The compound, known as DT-109, works by reducing harmful gut bacteria, protecting the intestinal lining, and preventing inflammatory substances from reaching the liver. According to findings published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation, this approach successfully reversed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in animal models, offering a promising new strategy for treating a disease that remains difficult to manage.

MASH affects approximately 7% of the world's population. It is a severe form of fatty liver disease in which excess fat accumulates in the liver, causing inflammation and cellular damage. Over time, the condition can progress to cirrhosis, which involves extensive liver scarring, as well as liver cancer and liver failure. Although treatment options have improved in recent years, effective therapies remain limited.

"We see clear evidence that DT-109 protects the gut epithelial barrier, reducing the systemic influx of harmful microbial products that are thought to contribute to MASH development and progression," said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., senior author of the study and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
"This compound shows benefits to the gastrointestinal system and has great potential as a treatment for MASH."
How Harmful Gut Bacteria Can Trigger Liver Damage

Chen's research team had previously demonstrated that DT-109, a glycine-based tripeptide, could improve MASH in animal studies. A tripeptide is a small molecule made from three amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. What remained unclear was exactly how the compound produced its protective effects.
The latest research provides an explanation, revealing how changes in gut bacteria can set off a chain reaction that damages the liver and how DT-109 can interrupt that process.
Before examining the drug's effects, the scientists confirmed an important contributor to MASH: excessive growth of Clostridium perfringens, a bacterium that produces ammonia inside the intestines.

When ammonia levels rise, they can damage the gut's protective inner lining. Normally, this intestinal barrier helps prevent potentially harmful substances from escaping the digestive tract and entering the bloodstream.

As the barrier weakens, however, toxins and other products generated by gut microbes can travel to the liver. Once there, they can provoke inflammation and activate immune defenses in ways that worsen liver damage.

One response involves the excessive activation of CD8+ T cells, immune cells that normally help the body destroy infected or abnormal cells. When these cells become overactive, they can contribute to the inflammatory processes associated with MASH.
The findings help explain why a disease centered in the liver can be strongly influenced by events occurring elsewhere in the digestive system.
Experimental Drug Repairs the Gut and Protects the Liver
Through a series of experiments, researchers discovered that DT-109 disrupts this damaging cycle by improving the intestinal environment and reinforcing the gut's protective barrier.

In both mice and nonhuman primates, the compound reduced levels of Clostridium perfringens and lowered ammonia production in the intestines. These changes helped strengthen the intestinal lining, limiting the movement of harmful microbial substances into the body and reducing their potential to damage the liver.

The results were particularly encouraging in nonhuman primates, whose liver biology and gut microbial communities more closely resemble those of humans than those of mice. In these animals, DT-109 reduced liver inflammation and lessened the severity of MASH.
Together, the findings show how targeting harmful processes in the gut can produce beneficial effects in the liver, even though the drug acts primarily within the gastrointestinal system.

"DT-109 connects microbiota modulation with liver protection by restoring gut barrier integrity and limiting the systemic translocation of ammonia and other pro-inflammatory microbial products within the gut-liver axis," said Jifeng Zhang, Ph.D., co-author and research professor of cardiovascular medicine at U-M Medical School.
"We also found that DT-109 primarily acts in the gastrointestinal tract, but its reach stretches much further."

The gut-liver axis refers to the close biological relationship between the digestive tract and the liver. Substances absorbed from the intestines travel to the liver through the bloodstream, making liver health particularly sensitive to changes in gut bacteria and intestinal barrier function.
By targeting this connection, DT-109 may offer a way to address some of the processes driving liver inflammation rather than focusing exclusively on damage that has already occurred.
Potential Benefits Beyond Fatty Liver Disease
Researchers believe the compound's ability to protect the intestinal barrier could make it useful against other conditions involving inflammation and metabolic dysfunction.
Previous research has shown that DT-109 can reduce the formation of atherosclerotic plaques and prevent vascular calcification in nonhuman primates.

Atherosclerotic plaques are deposits of fat and other substances that accumulate inside artery walls, potentially restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of cardiovascular problems. Vascular calcification occurs when calcium builds up in blood vessel walls, making them less flexible and contributing to cardiovascular disease.

These findings suggest that DT-109 could eventually have applications in treating both liver and cardiovascular conditions, an important possibility because metabolic disorders often affect multiple organs.

The researchers are also interested in whether the compound could help people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a group of chronic conditions that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Because problems with the intestinal barrier are associated with several gastrointestinal disorders, a treatment that strengthens this barrier might have benefits beyond protecting the liver. However, additional research will be needed to determine whether DT-109 is effective against these conditions.
A Promising Treatment That Still Needs Human Trials

Despite the encouraging results, DT-109 remains an experimental treatment. Its ability to reverse MASH has been demonstrated in animal models, but researchers have not yet established whether it can safely and effectively produce similar benefits in humans.

The next phase of research will involve further evaluation of the compound, with the goal of advancing it toward clinical trials. Those studies will be essential for determining its safety, appropriate use, and potential effectiveness in patients.

"This study presents novel evidence about the pathogenesis of MASH and provides excitement about a therapeutic avenue to explore for a condition that remains difficult to treat," said Elliot Tapper, M.D., Academic Director of Hepatology at Michigan Medicine.
"What patients with MASH need is a safe and effective therapy capable of improving their liver and heart health - of course we are excited about these developments."

The discovery highlights an important shift in how scientists are approaching fatty liver disease. By addressing harmful gut bacteria and restoring the intestinal barrier, researchers may be able to protect the liver through a treatment that acts primarily outside the organ itself.

If future human studies confirm the benefits seen in animals, DT-109 could offer a new therapeutic option for patients with severe fatty liver disease while potentially addressing cardiovascular complications as well.
Ying Zhao, Oren Rom, Jifeng Zhang, and Y. Eugene Chen are listed as inventors on a patent application (Tripeptides and treatment of metabolic, cardiovascular, and inflammatory disorders).

Chen is also an inventor of DT-109. The University of Michigan holds the patent for the compound and has licensed it to Diapin Therapeutics. Both Chen and the university have an ownership interest in Diapin, which supplied DT-109 for the research and is continuing its development.

The human study protocol, all amendments, and the informed consent form received approval from the Institutional Review Boards at the participating sites. These included the First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (approval number: XJTU1AF2023LSK330), the Institutional Review Board of Jinan University (approval number: 2016-017), and the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster (approval number: UW 20-700).

All experimental procedures involving nonhuman primates were approved by the Laboratory Animal Care Committee of Xi'an Jiaotong University (approval number: 20191278) and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Spring Biological Technology Development Co., Ltd. (approval number: 201901). The study was conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

Depending on the time of year, your location and the weather, your hopes to see the night sky in real life might not be as easy as heading into the backyard and peering up. That's why one of the best star projectors might be the solution.

That's why we've picked out six star projectors that actually deliver scientifically accurate images, from projections of the northern hemisphere to breathtaking pictures from the Hubble Space Telescope.

Any one of these will turn your home into a private planetarium. Each comes with several swappable images, and you can purchase additional slides/discs for the Homestar and Pococo models. If you're seeking to stimulate a child's interest in space and STEM or just take your friends on a journey through space, these are the scientifically accurate projectors to purchase.

paras.en: On Episode 232 of This Week In Space, Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik are joined by Chelsea Gohd, former writer for NASA/JPL and now with Space.com, to talk about the recent large data dump from the Artemis II mission.

What was included? Why is this new data important? What observations were made, and what discoveries might result from them? What kind of annotations and notes did the astronauts include that make these observations uniquely valuable?
And finally, we talk about Artemis III - what is the mission profile and what are the stakes for SpaceX and Blue Origin?

This Week in Space covers the new space age. Every Friday we take a deep dive into a fascinating topic. What's happening with the new race to the moon and other planets? When will SpaceX really send people to Mars?

Rod Pyle is an author, journalist, television producer and Editor-in-Chief of Ad Astra magazine. He has written 18 books on space history, exploration, and development, including Space 2.0, Innovation the NASA Way, Interplanetary Robots, Blueprint for a Battlestar, Amazing Stories of the Space Age, First On the Moon, and Destination Mars

In a previous life, Rod produced numerous documentaries and short films for The History Channel, Discovery Communications, and Disney. He also worked in visual effects on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and the Battlestar Galactica reboot, as well as various sci-fi TV pilots. Responsible for Space.com's editorial vision, Tariq Malik has been the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com since 2019 and has covered space news and science for 18 years. He joined the Space.com team in 2001, first as an intern and soon after as a full-time spaceflight reporter covering human spaceflight, exploration, astronomy and the night sky. He became Space.com's managing editor in 2009. As on-air talent has presented space stories on CNN, Fox News, NPR and others.

Tariq is an Eagle Scout (yes, he earned the Space Exploration merit badge), a Space Camp veteran (4 times as a kid, once as an adult), and has taken the ultimate "vomit comet" ride while reporting on zero-gravity fires. Before joining Space.com, he served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering city and education beats. He has journalism degrees from the University of Southern California and New York University.

Space.com is the premier source of space exploration, innovation and astronomy news, chronicling (and celebrating) humanity's ongoing expansion across the final frontier. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 17, 2016: Private Antares rocket returns to flight after catastrophic launch explosion
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On Oct. 17, 2016, Orbital ATK (now Northrop Grumman Space Systems) returned to flight, successfully launching a cargo shipment to the International Space Station (ISS) after its previous cargo mission failed to launch.

The private spaceflight company was contracted by NASA to fly cargo to the ISS, and stakes were high for this launch. Orbital ATK's last attempt nearly two years earlier ended in a catastrophic explosion a few seconds after liftoff.

Despite some delays, the newly upgraded Antares rocket flawlessly blasted off into the night sky from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. Six days later, the Cygnus cargo spacecraft arrived at the ISS to deliver food, supplies and science experiments to the crew.

For the International Space Station to be able to sustain a continuous human occupancy, periodic cargo deliveries are needed. Russia fulfills part of this requirement with its Progress spacecraft, and both ESA (European Space Agency) and JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) have contributed with their Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) and H-II Transfer Vehicle (HTV), respectively.

For its part, NASA contracted with Orbital (today, Northrop Grumman) and SpaceX to fly commercial resupply service missions. Both were needed to keep the U.S. operating segment of the station well supplied and with the science and research materials needed for the crew's work.

Though adjustments can be made to go without one or more of these vehicles for a short period of time, the Progress, Cygnus and Dragon are key components of the ISS's continuous operation. So returning a vehicle to flight after a catastrophic exploration is important to well-being of the International Space Station program.
As it happened, Antares would fly another 12 times before having to stand down again to be redesigned, but that is for a different This Day in Space entry.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

This milestone underscores our ability to provide cutting-edge technology that meets the demands of international space missions.

In a market that moves fast, the ASTRO HP optical head provides the perfect balance: high performance thanks to the radiation-hard Faintstar2 detector, the very fast optics in a compact, lightweight design optimized for small and medium-sized, high-performance satellites.

articles.title: Agile Space Industries Expands to Seattle Area with New Bellevue Office
articles.author: Agile Space Industries

paras.en: BELLEVUE, Wash., Oct. 15, 2026 — Agile Space Industries, a leading provider of in-space chemical propulsion solutions, has expanded into the Seattle metropolitan area with the opening of a new office in Bellevue, Washington. The expansion builds on Agile’s continued growth, extending its engineering capabilities and strengthening its presence in one of the nation’s most established aerospace and technology markets.

Located at Sunset North in Bellevue, the new 5,470-square-foot office will initially accommodate 7 employees, with the capacity to grow to approximately 30 as Agile expands its regional operations. Agile Chief Technology Officer Jake Mills will be based at the Bellevue office, reinforcing the company’s commitment to establishing a strong engineering and leadership presence in the region.

“Seattle has a remarkable concentration of aerospace talent, innovative companies and organizations advancing the space industry,” said Jake Mills, chief technology officer at Agile Space Industries. “Establishing a presence here allows us to tap into that expertise, strengthen industry relationships and build on the capabilities we’re developing across Agile to support our customers and their missions.”

The Bellevue office will focus on engineering and program management, supporting the development and delivery of advanced propulsion systems for government and commercial space missions. As the team grows, Agile expects to broaden its technical expertise and support an expanding range of propulsion programs.

Beyond its engineering talent, the Seattle region offers an established network of aerospace companies, industry partners and investors. Agile’s presence in this ecosystem creates opportunities to strengthen customer relationships, develop new partnerships and engage with the broader business and investment community as the company pursues its long-term growth objectives.

The expansion also creates opportunities for experienced aerospace professionals looking to work on complex propulsion challenges in a collaborative, hands-on engineering environment. Agile’s teams contribute to programs spanning early development through qualified flight hardware, with the opportunity to help shape technologies supporting the next generation of space missions.

The Bellevue office joins Agile’s headquarters in Durango, Colorado, and operations in Pennsylvania and Oklahoma. Together, these locations support Agile’s growing capabilities in propulsion design, manufacturing and testing, positioning the company to serve an expanding range of commercial and government space customers.

Agile Space Industries develops advanced chemical propulsion solutions that enable spacecraft to move, maneuver, and operate in space. From early concepts to qualified flight hardware, Agile brings together propulsion expertise, additive manufacturing, and in-house testing to rapidly solve complex challenges and accelerate development. Agile partners with leading aerospace companies and the U.S. Government on spacecraft and launch vehicle programs. Learn more at agilespaceindustries.com.

articles.title: WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

paras.en: WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to support Kenya’s efforts to contain Ebola after a second person tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus, the UN agency’s representative in the country said on Thursday.
The patient, a 39-year-old man, is a relative of Kenya’s first case – related to the ongoing deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – who died in hospital on 5 October.
He was among contacts who were placed in quarantine and developed symptoms on 13 October.

“I congratulate the Government for taking this important step to ensure that contacts are listed and quarantined,” WHO Representative Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo told UN News in Nairobi, a day after the Ministry of Health confirmed the new case.

“But to defeat this disease, it's not about the Government, it is not about partners It is about everybody,” she insisted. “We all have a role to play and if each one of us plays our part, then we should be able to contain the disease and stop community spread.”
Kenya’s first Ebola patient and fatality was a local man who had been living in the DRC, where the record outbreak continues to spread in the east.
He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on 3 October and died in hospital two days later.
Dr. Kimambo commended health authorities who “cast the net very wide” to identify people who had come into contact with him – whether in the air or on the ground.
The more than 40 people included airline passengers and crew, airplane cleaners, airport workers, baggage handlers and immigration officials, as well as health personnel and family members.

Most are in quarantine, while a few low-risk contacts have self-quarantined and are being monitored. Meanwhile, every effort is being made to reach six passengers who have been difficult to locate because they have foreign phone numbers.

Even before the first case , WHO and the Kenyan Government were stepping up Ebola preparedness after the outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. Neighbouring Uganda also confronted the disease, with any outbreak officially ruled out in late August.

Teams are working across all areas, including surveillance and contact tracing. WHO has also brought in a senior incident manager who participated in the Ebola response in Uganda, as well as other experts.

“We are building on the work that we started during the preparedness phase, so case management and IPC (infection prevention and control) are critical at this time in the quarantine centres,” Dr. Kimambo said.

WHO also continues to provide assistance to Kenya in various other ways. The UN agency has donated some $70,000 worth of supplies, including IPC and laboratory items, since the first Ebola case was identified.
Additionally, more than 4,000 health workers have been trained, including for screenings at ports of entry.

While Dr. Kimambo said there still is no need to impose travel restrictions or close national borders, she underlined the importance of appropriate screening to identify travellers who may pose a health risk.
Preventing Ebola begins with understanding how the disease is transmitted, she said, which is through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.
She reiterated the advice to practice regular handwashing, use hand sanitizer and avoid shaking hands.

As Ebola symptoms include fever, vomiting and diarrhoea – which mimic symptoms of malaria and other diseases – she stressed the need to seek medical care quickly. In the interim, Kenyans are urged to keep calm and stay safe.

“I think one is not to over panic and be very fearful because we do not have community spread,” she said. “But two, let us be responsible. Whoever is sick, let’s make sure we go to a health facility and get care. And also, let us ensure that we take IPC measures.”

articles.title: Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations

paras.en: Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations

Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global hunger monitor report released on Thursday.
UN agency heads are calling for emergency support to stem the crisis, as a separate report details serious human rights violations – from public floggings to a new ban on demonstrations.
- 15.9 million Afghans are facing acute food insecurity
- 3.4 million are experiencing emergency food insecurity conditions, which precedes famine, and conditions are expected to worsen
- New UN report on human rights in Afghanistan reveals serious violations, from public floggings to a fresh ban on demonstrations

Record acute malnutrition levels for the August–October period have seen hunger levels grow for millions of Afghans – according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global initiative aimed at informing decisions based on five phases of food security.

Economic pressures are straining households nationwide, contributing to more than 32 per cent of the population facing crisis-level acute food insecurity phase three or above, including 3.4 million people experiencing emergency phase four conditions.
The current deterioration is driven by disease outbreaks and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions, compounded by sharply reduced access to nutrition services, the report found.

The situation is expected to worsen from November to April during the winter lean season, when nearly 19.2 million people are projected to face phase three or above, including five million people in emergency food insecurity conditions.
Acute malnutrition is also set to grow significantly, with 4.04 million children under age five projected to need treatment between January and December 2027.
“Although improved rainfall and better agricultural production have supported food availability, declining humanitarian assistance is reducing households’ ability to cope,” the report warned.

The World Food Programme (WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) issued a stark message on Thursday, calling for urgent funding to scale up food assistance, emergency agricultural support and malnutrition prevention and treatment.

“We still have a window to act, but it is closing fast,” WFP country director John Aylieff said. “With urgent support, families can get through the winter with dignity. Without it, many will face impossible choices no parent should have to make.”
FAO representative Richard Trenchard said families need opportunities to earn a dependable living that “helps them withstand the next shock” and support to get through this winter.

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) on Thursday reported the continued erosion of basic human rights across the country between July and September, with women and girls bearing the brunt of restrictions imposed by Taliban authorities.

Girls’ school ban: Girls remain barred from formal education beyond grade six. Asked about the ban, a Taliban spokesperson said that “problems and considerations” had to be taken into account from the perspective of Sharia law.

Women arrested, detained or cautioned: UNAMA documented more than 50 cases related to the hijab, mostly in Herat and Kabul. In one case, a 13-year-old girl was held overnight. Women were also blocked from entering health clinics and markets without a male guardian, or mahram.

Arbitrary arrests and detentions: The mission recorded at least 443 cases and 97 incidents of ill-treatment by virtue and vice inspectors over offences including hijab violations, trimmed beards, skipped prayers and listening to music.

Judicial corporal punishment: While the de facto Supreme Court stopped publicly announcing such cases on its social media account and website in April, UNAMA documented public lashings of 22 men and six women on charges including theft and adultery, and the arrest of 14 former security force members, with at least four others killed.

Media and civic freedom curtailed: Several outlets were suspended without clear reasons or appeal procedures. A journalist arrested in July 2025 remains in custody without conviction. A new police law, published in August, bans all demonstrations.

Cross-border violence: Since October 2025, 512 civilians have been killed and 1,236 injured, with 33 casualties in the latest quarter, including children killed in Pakistani airstrikes on homes in Kunar and Helmand.

articles.title: Arsenal booed after Birmingham draw as pressure builds on Slegers

paras.en: Arsenal Women vs Birmingham City Women; Barclays Women's Super League
Arsenal Women vs Birmingham City Women. Barclays Women's Super League.
Arsenal 1-1 Birmingham: Olivia Smith stunner saves Gunners from shocking defeat but pressure intensifies on Renee Slegers

Report and free match highlights as Arsenal draw 1-1 with Birmingham City at the Emirates Stadium; Olivia Smith's stunner cancels out Oceane Hurtre's opener; Arsenal with just one win in six WSL games
Pressure continued to mount on Renee Slegers as Arsenal were booed off the pitch following their 1-1 draw with Birmingham at the Emirates.
Arsenal went into the international break with just five points from their opening five WSL games after the 4-2 defeat with Manchester City, and just one win in six in all competitions.
A home game against newly-promoted Birmingham, who themselves had mustered just two league draws all campaign, seemed like the scenario to return to winning ways.

After Alessia Russo struck the post with a fabulous diving header in the first half, the Gunners were left stunned as they were hit on the break early in the second, allowing September's player of the month Oceane Hurtre to poke the visitors ahead.

Birmingham's resolve was tested, with Sophie Baggaley making a superb save to maintain the lead. However, seconds later she was beaten by an incredible Olivia Smith strike to pull Slegers' side level.
Arsenal pushed for a late winner but a combination of Baggaley and their inefficiency in front of goal that has plagued them all season ensured they went winless in five WSL games for the first time.
It resulted in boos at the full-time whistle, as questions over Slegers' future intensify.
14: SAVE! Cooney-Cross' smart half-volley kept out by Baggaley.
18: OVER! Russo gifted a chance after Baggaley's poor pass, but attempted lob goes over.
38: POST! Russo comes agonisingly close to converting excellent Williamson cross.
50: OVER! Holmberg impressive run ends in her striking over the bar.
53: GOAL! Arsenal shell-shocked as Hurtre gives Birmingham lead on the counter.
65: HUGE SAVE! Baggaley denies Baum from point-blank range.

76: OVER! Smith snatches at big chance to put Arsenal ahead.
Slegers: If I can't help the team, a change is needed
Arsenal boss Renee Slegers speaking in her post-match press conference:
"Everything I want is for the best of us and for the success of all these players. So, that's heavily on my mind and I still believe I can impact and help the team forward.
"But, if that's not the case anymore, then a change needs to happen, but I have belief in knowing where we can go with this team and it's been really tough.
"Like I just said, if it had been all negative and we hadn't been looking like Arsenal but that's not the case.
"There's some details that we need to get right and those details are costing us right now. Those margins are costing us and I believe that if we get that right, it'll be good."

"It's been such an interesting start to the season for Arsenal. I think they are left with so many questions and no answers right now, but they are not playing badly. They're not failing to create chances.
"If Manchester City and Chelsea win tomorrow, you would almost write them out of the title race.

"If they had won today they might've found a bit of momentum. I genuinely think the failure to win today has pushed them out of a title race. That was not what Renee Slegers' mission was this season."

articles.title: McIlroy drops out of contention at DP World India Championship

paras.en: DP World India Championship: Rory McIlroy drops 10 shots off the lead as Eugenio Chacarra moving into position for another big win
Rory McIlroy drops out of contention - 10 shots off leader Eugenio Chacarra - with Saturday's play suspended because of fading light, with most of the field yet to finish their third round
Spain's Eugenio Chacarra holds the lead at the DP World India Championship with Rory McIlroy dropping out of contention after play was suspended for the day on Saturday.
Chacarra was leading by two strokes on 14 under when Saturday's play was suspended because of fading light, with most of the field yet to finish their third round.
The Spaniard was four under for his round after 11 holes, having started out in the halfway lead after completing a second-round 67 early Saturday.
Joost Luiten was four under after 12 holes and Angel Hidalgo four under after 11 holes, with both players tied for second place on 12 under par.
Daniel Hillier, Adrian Meronk and Scott Jamieson were a further shot back.
Patrick Reed and McIlroy - battling with Chacarra for the season-long Race to Dubai title - were eight and 10 shots off the lead, respectively.
Chacarra earned one of the biggest wins of his career in India last year, triumphing at the Hero Indian Open - where he was playing on an invitation - to earn his full status on the European tour.
He had previously been on the LIV Golf circuit.
Play will restart at 6.35am local time on Sunday, with Chacarra needing to play the remaining seven holes of his third round as well as his entire final round.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan cheered in first joint appearance since returning to U.K.
articles.author: Laura Saravia

paras.en: LONDON — Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.
Harry, 42, and Meghan, 45, were visiting three charities in Nottingham, as they look to rebuild their image in Britain six years after walking away from royal life.

Nottingham, a city in central England known as the setting for the famous “Robin Hood” legend, holds a special place in the couple’s history as the place where they made their first joint public appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.
“It’s almost a full-circle moment because it looks very much like a royal engagement,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said.

The events Thursday began with a visit to the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity in Nottingham that Harry has visited before, including just last year. They were greeted by a cheering crowd, filled largely with young children.
Harry and Meghan, who wore a long burgundy coat, stopped to take selfies, give hugs and shake hands. They also spent a few minutes talking to members of the public and the children.
The couple were also due to visit the region’s biggest food bank, Himmah, and Epic Partners, which offers disadvantaged young people mentoring programs, sports and education.
Noting that the couple will be visiting a charity Harry has a “long history with,” Nash said they were certain to “get a warm reception” given their “long connection with it.”
But they have not always received such a warm welcome since their return to the U.K. with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.
The couple remain locked in a public row with Buckingham Palace about their status and their lack of publicly funded police protection.

A letter sent on behalf of King Charles III to senior government and military officials confirmed Harry and Meghan remain nonworking members of the royal family. A spokesperson for the couple told NBC News they were “surprised” by the letter, though they accepted that status when they left Britain for a quieter life in Montecito, California, an affluent coastal enclave in Santa Barbara.

Their relationship with the royal family has been strained in the years since, with the couple leveling explosive allegations of racism and bullying in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.”
News of their return to the U.K. sent shock waves through the British media, and the couple have faced other complications as they settle back into British life.

“It was a bit of a bumpy road for Harry and Meghan,” Nash said. “They had to move their children from their school after just two days, but I’m told they’re settling in well now and Archie and Lili are very happy at their new school.”
The couple’s royal-style visit to Nottingham will renew questions about their security.
With or without it, Nash said, “this is them dipping their toe back in the water” and “nothing’s stopping them.”
“They don’t need the palace’s permission to do this,” she said.

articles.title: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.author: The Associated Press

paras.en: EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.

With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said.

Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.

Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan.
“He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked.
“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Some Albertans say the vote shouldn’t have been called
Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.

Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.

“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.
Political leaders unite against separation
Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada.
“Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.

Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

articles.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous nodule from his right lung.

The pontiff, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided before spending a couple of minutes speaking with well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling Pope figure before getting in a car and being driven back to the Vatican.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement, before the Leo left the building mid-afternoon.
He is expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.
Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.
“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

articles.title: Starlink speed restrictions ground interceptors as Russian strikes batter Ukraine

paras.en: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the country's interceptor systems are ineffective due to speed restrictions imposed by Starlink.
He said when used in EU territory, the system worked at higher speeds.
It comes as US President Donald Trump pauses incoming sanctions against Russia, after agreeing to purchase diesel from the country.
Ukraine is now unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of a Starlink speed restriction, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.
He said any restrictions would have been set by the US military and US President Donald Trump.
Mr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues, adding he was discussing it with US officials.
He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.
Earlier this week Ukraine experienced similar issues, with Starlink owner Elon Musk responding by insisting his firm had nothing to do with the speed limits.
Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike
President Zelenskyy said Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.
Ukraine's air force said Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight.
All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.
Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water.
Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

President Zelenskyy has also urged supporters to speak out in defence of new US sanctions against Russia, hours after Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House decision has further raised fears Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults.
Mr Zelenskyy described Mr Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticise the US leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Mr Zelenskyy wrote.
He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived.
"This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.
Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin
Named after late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia's against Ukraine.
The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
President Trump personally signed the legislation last month, two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.
The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement Mr Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,"

Mr Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Mr Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Mr Trump's war on Iran.

articles.title: Burning buildings and tear gas mark 29th day of French student protests

paras.en: Protesters have clashed with police across France during continued nationwide rallies over education and the cost of living.
A government building stormed in Marseille had the anarchy symbol spray painted on walls, while buildings were set alight in Lyon.
The clashes come in the lead up to France's presidential election in April next year.
Protesters clashed with police across France during nationwide rallies over education and the cost of living, as the country heads towards a presidential election.
In Paris, police fired a water cannon and tear gas after hundreds of protesters — most wearing face masks and some setting off fireworks — confronted them at several locations on Saturday.
The tourist office in Lyon was set on fire on Saturday, and offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in Paris had windows broken when protesters threw projectiles, French media reported.
"We're taking the Bastille," one demonstrator shouted in Marseille as masked protesters rammed the door of the mayor's offices with security barriers.
The cry is a reference to the 1789 storming of a fortress during the French Revolution.
Several then entered the town hall, one spray painting an anarchist "A" symbol on an inside wall, before police intervened.
"We're here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality," said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.
Thousands of demonstrators converged for a march through Paris, cutting main roads and prompting authorities to close metro stations in the centre.
The protests are piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron's government after weeks of student demonstrations turned violent.
The country's Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests against Mr Macron's government eight years ago over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website set up by organisers.

More than 32,000 protesters took part in some 140 actions nationwide outside Paris shortly after midday on Saturday and police detained more than 160 people nationwide, a source at the interior ministry told AFP.
In Paris, where authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.
There has been public criticism over the police's perceived disproportionate response.
In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.

Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.
"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he told AFP.
"At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren't," said Franck, a civil servant in his forties who would not give his surname.
Franck was protesting in the central town of Gueret with around 300 people, a quarter of them high school students.
"We can't take it anymore, we're suffocating," he added.
Around 45 per cent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
Purchasing power in France has dwindled since 2024, while the price of fuel has soared since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year.
The eurozone's second largest economy is struggling to reign in its public debt, projected next year to reach more than 120 per cent of GDP, which is double the EU limit of 60 per cent.
Economists say significant debt reduction will come only with major reforms, such as sharply curtailing France's generous pension system.
President Macron on Friday evening called "for calm and respect", adding the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property".
France's far-left and far-right parties have both capitalised upon the unrest.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration.
Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.

articles.title: Pope Leo leaves hospital for Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery

paras.en: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
Pope Leo has returned to the Vatican from hospital.
It comes after the 71-year old underwent surgery for lung cancer four days ago.
The pope's doctors said he could return home following his latest blood tests and chest imaging.

articles.title: This West Bank teen feared he wouldn't survive the year. Now, he's dead
articles.author: Tom Parry

paras.en: This West Bank teen feared he wouldn't survive the year. Now, he's dead
Omar Nassan, 17, spoke to CBC News in April and was killed amid violence in September

The cemetery in the West Bank village of Al Mughayyir is dotted with burial sites draped with the Palestinian flag, marking the graves of local men and boys killed in clashes over the years with Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces.
It was one of the places 17-year-old Omar Nassan insisted that CBC News visit back in April.

Omar was a student at the local boys' school where a gunman, later identified as an Israeli military reservist, opened fire this spring, killing two Palestinians: 32-year-old Jihad Abu Naim and 14-year-old Aws al-Nassan. Both now lay in that small cemetery overlooking hills, fields and a busy roadway.
Omar and Aws had been good friends, and he talked about life in Al Mughayyir with a deep sense of frustration and fatalism.

"To be honest, I didn’t tell this to anyone … but I already accepted death. I’m going to be dead," Omar said. "I lost my friend and he’s not the first first friend I lose, whether it’s getting killed or in prison. He’s not the first or the last friend I lose, so I already accept death. I’m going to be next."
Omar said many young men in the village felt the same way. The stress of life in the Occupied West Bank, combined with the constant threat of violence, had worn them down.
"It can’t get more dangerous," he said. "We’re used to that now. It’s our life."
Omar’s words on that April afternoon proved tragically prescient.

The cemetery in the village of Al Mughayyir is dotted with burial sites draped with the Palestinian flag, marking the graves of local men and boys killed in clashes with Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces. (CBC)

On the evening of Sept. 2, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) deployed troops to Al Mughayyir to back up Israeli police responding to a disturbance over missing livestock. Palestinian villagers routinely accuse Israeli settlers of stealing sheep and allowing their own flocks to graze on Palestinian land.
- Prosecutors charge Israeli settler for killing Palestinian activist in West Bank
- Gunman kills 1, wounds 5 in drive-by attacks in Israel near West Bank border

The IDF says it was brought in to retrieve animals owned by Israeli civilians when a violent riot broke out. In a statement, the military says soldiers encountered what it calls "terrorists" hurling cinderblocks and stones. The soldiers fired on what the IDF calls "key instigators" and that "hits were identified."
Two young Palestinians died that night: 16-year-old Khalil Abu Alia and 17-year-old Omar Nassan.

Omar’s family says he was shot just outside their home in Al Mughayyir. His father, Mohammad Nassan, says his son was struck by three bullets and managed to stumble a few steps before crumpling to the ground. He says an ambulance took his son to hospital but medics were unable to save his life.
"My back is broken," Nassan said of his son’s death, in an interview with CBC News. "He helped me in every detail of my life. "
Omar Nassan's parents, Mohammad and Rania, say their son was struck by three bullets during a melee between Israeli Defence Forces and Palestinian protesters in September. (CBC)
Omar’s mother, Rania, says her son loved to eat, did well at school and had a natural talent for working with computers. Omar learned English, she says, at school in her native country, Egypt.

On the night Omar died, Rania Nassan says she heard screaming and chanting outside her home and rushed to lock the door. She says Omar ran after her and begged her to let him go downstairs to see what was happening.
"I opened the door and told him to take care of himself," she said. "And that was it."
As the melee in the street continued, Rania says she began receiving text messages from neighours saying Omar had been injured. Women from the village eventually came to tell her that he was dead.
"I felt that my soul was separated," Rania said, describing that moment. "I felt like the mountains would not bear the news."

Rania says Omar was deeply affected by the loss of his friend in the school shooting in April. He confided to her his feelings that he could be the next to die. She regrets not talking to him more about it.
Palestinian youth are seen on the streets of Al Mughayyir. (CBC)
The Nassan family believes Omar was shot by an IDF sniper soon after he left his home. The IDF won’t confirm that.

As for the shooting at the school in April, the IDF says the case is currently under review by the Military Advocate General’s Corps, but won’t say whether the review or its ruling will be made public.

Marzouq Abu Naim, whose son Jihad was killed in the school attack, is a member of the Al Mughayyir Village Council. By his count, Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces have killed 11 people in the community, eight of them under the age of 18.
The United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs lists nine Palestinian deaths in Al Mughayyir since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
Abu Naim says after that attack, in which more than 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 taken hostage, the IDF began treating people in his village far more harshly.

"Before October 7, the army would keep us apart when there was a problem between the settlers and us," he said. "After October 7, we wished that the army would not come. Because if the army came, the problem would be more difficult. The army sprays tear gas at us and the army shoots."
Abu Naim's son is buried in Al Mughayyir's cemetery. Half a year after showing it to CBC News, Omar Nassan is buried there, too.
Omar's father says the family is planning to install a monument to remember him, but for now, it's just a simple gravesite draped, like others in the cemetery, with a Palestinian flag.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia hours after Trump paused them

paras.en: Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia hours after Trump paused them
Ukraine's leader also said Moscow carried out massive strike on energy infrastructure

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters on Saturday to speak out in defence of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House’s decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.
Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but he did not directly criticize the U.S. leader. Tensions between Ukraine and Washington have deepened in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on social media platform X.

He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived. "This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.
'Severe consequences' from strikes: Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy also said on Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.
Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the nearly five-year-old war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russia claims it has taken control of another town

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Saturday its forces had taken control of eight more Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia in eastern Donetsk region, news agency Interfax reported.

The town, southwest of the key centres of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, has been under sustained Russian attack for some time. But Ukraine's General Staff denied Russia's claim and said on Saturday that Ukrainian forces remained in control of the eastern town of Dobropillia.

In an emailed statement, General Staff spokesperson Andriy Kovaliov said Ukraine also rejected Russia's claim that Russian forces had captured more than 1,800 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since Sept. 1.
Russia's Defence Ministry also said it had struck Ukrainian drone storage sites and transport infrastructure used by Ukraine's armed forces over the past 24 hours.

articles.title: Hundreds arrested, tear gas deployed in chaotic protests across France over cost of living concerns

paras.en: Hundreds arrested, tear gas deployed in chaotic protests across France over cost of living concerns
- Nationwide demonstrations are taking place in France today over the cost of living, with "yellow vest" groups, students and trade unions calling on people to take to the streets.
- More than 272 arrests have been made across the country, while hundreds of youth are clashing with police in the Place de la République in Paris.
- Outside of Paris, French police say 140 protests are happening so far Saturday, with 32,800 people involved.
- The main tourism centre in the southeastern French town of Lyon, about 460 kilometres from Paris, was set on fire during Saturday's protests.
- France has been grappling with weeks of unrest as student-led protests calling for better conditions for learning have led to widespread school disruptions, arrests and violence.

- October 17 France at 'major turning point' says mayor of Paris suburb Chris Brown With tear gas filling the streets of Paris and vandalized vehicles smouldering around the Place de la République, France is facing yet another moment of reckoning. Many of those occupying the streets today belong to La France Insoumise (France Unbowed), the country's hard-left coalition that openly supports direct confrontation with the government of President Emmanuel Macron. On the other side, opponents of the unrest from the political centre and right are pushing back. Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, blamed what he called "anti-cop militias" for the violence and declared his solid backing of the security forces. I spoke to a prominent civic leader about the extreme polarization gripping the nation, and he offered few clear solutions for how the country moves forward. "France is coming to a major turning point," said Bally Bagayoko, the left-wing mayor of the working-class Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. Bagayoko has become a central figure in this crisis. He is a fierce advocate for French high schoolers who have spent weeks blockading schools to demand more government education funding. Earlier this month, a video went viral showing Bagayoko physically wedging himself between a line of riot police and young students in Paris to dial down the threat of violence. "Today, unfortunately, this France is in sadness," Bagayoko told me. "It is unable to provide concrete answers to the legitimate demands of high schoolers.” Triggered by severe gridlock over national budget and austerity measures, France has faced a rapid succession of hung parliaments and short-lived governments. With a high-stakes presidential election looming next spring, today’s chaotic scenes appear destined to entrench the country's political paralysis even deeper.

paras.en: - Why French student protesters have taken up the slogan, 'Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres' Jillian Kestler-D'Amours You may have seen the viral phrase "Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" on posters, spraypainted on walls or shared in memes as France's student protest movement has grown in recent weeks. But where exactly does the slogan — which translates to, "In the name of God, it's the darkness" — come from? It goes back to what the students say was an alleged attempt by French police to infiltrate the protests. A message was apparently posted to Snapchat by someone calling themselves "Mamadou." The message opened with the phrase "Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres," and went on to ask for more information about the planning of the protests. The message was widely shared — and mocked — online, and then it started to appear at the demonstrations, too. Greta Thunberg, the Swedish activist who joined the French protests earlier this week, also poked fun at the phrase in an Instagram video expressing support for French activist collective Œil au Beurre Noire.

Some are pulling concrete off the monument in the centre of the square and throwing the rock at lines of tactical police. Thousands of other demonstrators — most appearing to be members of the yellow vests — have begun marching to other parts of the city. We've seen a number of injured protesters being looked after by medics, but the total number of people hurt isn't clear.

During Saturday's protests, the main tourism centre in the southeastern French town of Lyon, about 460 kilometres from Paris, was set on fire. Images show black smoke billowing out of the building, with flames engulfing its interior. Nationwide, more than 160 people have been arrested so far, authorities say.

With the high schoolers, the outcry has grown particularly loud, partly because the vast majority of the thousands arrested in recent weeks are under 18 and because police riot control weapons are blamed for life-changing injuries suffered by some young teens. The latest unrest is marking the final months for the president, who is slated to leave his post in May of next year.

They also burned down a kiosk. When police tried to push hundreds of black-clad protesters back to let firefighters through, they were met with a hail of rocks and cans.

- More than 5,000 arrests and over 200 injured so far Kyle G. Brown A 15-year-old boy lost a hand during student protests across France calling for better school conditions. More than 5,000 young people have been arrested during the unrest, and dozens of schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister. Since the movement began last month, hundreds of schools have been blockaded. While the majority of protests have been peaceful, some have been marred by vandalism and violence. Police have made more than 5,000 arrests so far. More than 200 people have been injured since the student mobilization began, "whether in accidents … or due to injuries caused by troublemakers," said Education Minister Édouard Geffray. Police have also severely injured some people, including a youth who was blinded in one eye after being hit by a projectile. France has suspended the use of stun grenades after a 15-year-old boy in the north of the country lost his hand during a demonstration. Amnesty International condemned "the disproportionate use of force against secondary school protests," calling for police to de-escalate. At least 18 internal investigations into alleged police violence are underway.
